questions.stem: A 44 year old man has sudden, severe epigastric pain that began 3 hours ago and now affects his whole abdomen. He has had dyspepsia for months and smokes 20 a day. He takes no medications. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He lies still and his abdomen is rigid with reduced bowel sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden epigastric pain becoming generalised, with a board-like abdomen and a history of dyspepsia, is a perforated peptic ulcer; H. pylori is the likely cause without NSAIDs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Epigastric** to **generalised**, sudden, **rigid**, on a background of **dyspepsia**. No NSAIDs, so think H. pylori.

elim: RUQ pain with Murphy's sign; not a rigid abdomen within hours.
The amylase is normal.
The troponin is normal.
Pain radiates to the back with shock; he is not hypotensive.

steps.x: **D. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Sudden epigastric pain that generalises with a rigid abdomen = perforated peptic ulcer.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica on prednisolone takes ibuprofen for knee pain. She has had epigastric pain for 12 hours. She is tender in the epigastrium with mild guarding but no rigidity. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her erect chest X-ray is shown.

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Crescents of gas under both hemidiaphragms: pneumoperitoneum.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: NSAIDs plus steroids are a classic setup for a perforated peptic ulcer. Steroids blunt the signs, so the abdomen may not be rigid; free gas under the diaphragm makes the diagnosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**NSAID + steroid**, epigastric pain, and **free air under the diaphragm**. Steroids mask peritonism.

elim: Does not cause free intraperitoneal gas.
Would show consolidation, not gas under the diaphragm.
No free gas; pain is colicky RUQ.
A post-operative complication; she has had no surgery.

steps.x: **D. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Free air under the diaphragm + NSAID use = perforated peptic ulcer, even with soft-ish signs on steroids.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man returned from Nepal 3 weeks ago. He has had 2 weeks of rising fever, headache, dry cough, myalgia and constipation. Today he has sudden lower abdominal pain. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His abdomen is rigid. Blood cultures later grow Salmonella Typhi.
questions.q: Which part of the bowel has most likely perforated?
questions.e: Typhoid causes necrosis of Peyer's patches, which are concentrated in the terminal (distal) ileum, so this is where it perforates, typically in the second to third week.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which part of the bowel has most likely perforated? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: rising fever, headache, dry cough, myalgia and constipation
steps.x: Returned traveller, **typhoid** symptoms, then peritonitis: **Peyer's patches** necrose and perforate.

elim: Not where the lymphoid tissue targeted by typhoid is concentrated.
Typical of peptic ulcer perforation.
Has few Peyer's patches.
Typical of diverticular perforation.

steps.x: **E. Terminal ileum.** Typhoid perforation = terminal ileum (Peyer's patches).

questions.stem: A 25 year old man was the restrained driver in a car crash 14 hours ago. He has a seatbelt bruise across his lower abdomen. His pain has increased steadily and he has vomited. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He has generalised tenderness with guarding. CT shows free intraperitoneal gas and fluid between small bowel loops. The liver and spleen are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Trauma is a cause of GI perforation. A seatbelt injury with delayed peritonitis and extraluminal gas on CT is a small bowel perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Seatbelt injury**, **delayed** peritonism, and **extraluminal gas**: a hollow viscus has ruptured.

elim: The liver is normal on CT, and it would not cause free gas.
Retroperitoneal; would not usually give free intraperitoneal gas.
Haematuria and loin pain; no free gas.
The spleen is normal; it causes haemorrhage, not free gas.

steps.x: **D. Small bowel perforation.** Free gas after blunt trauma = hollow viscus (often small bowel) perforation.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer diagnosed 1 hour after the pain began. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has guarding and rebound tenderness. The junior doctor reassures the family because his blood pressure is normal.
questions.q: Which finding is most likely to appear only late in his illness?
questions.e: Hypotension is a late sign in GI perforation. A normal BP with tachycardia and peritonism does not mean the patient is safe.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which finding is most likely to appear only late in his illness? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
He already has **tachycardia**, guarding and rebound. A normal BP is reassuring only until it is not.

elim: An early sign of peritonism; he already has it.
Present from the start of peritonitis.
An early peritoneal sign; he already has it.
Usually early; he already has it.

steps.x: **B. Hypotension.** In perforation, hypotension is a late sign; do not be falsely reassured by a normal BP.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has a 3 month history of change in bowel habit, 6 kg weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia. He was awaiting a colonoscopy. Today he has sudden severe abdominal pain and his abdomen is rigid. CT shows an irregular stricturing sigmoid mass with adjacent free gas and pericolic lymph nodes, with no diverticula seen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his perforation?
questions.e: Red flags (weight loss, change in bowel habit, iron deficiency) with an irregular mass and nodes point to a perforated colorectal cancer; malignancy is a recognised cause of GI perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his perforation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: change in bowel habit, 6 kg weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia
steps.x: **Red flags** + **irregular mass** with nodes, and no diverticula.

elim: Unusual new onset at 73 with an irregular mass and nodes.
No diverticula are seen.
He has not yet had his colonoscopy.
The gas is next to a sigmoid mass, not the duodenum.

steps.x: **A. Colorectal malignancy.** Perforation with red flags and a mass = malignancy until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman in a care home is brought in more confused than usual. She takes naproxen for arthritis. Carers say she complained of tummy pain yesterday. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Her abdomen is distended and tender with reduced bowel sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Older patients with a perforated ulcer often present atypically with confusion, hypotension, distension and raised WCC/CRP/lactate. NSAID use is the clue.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: distended and tender with reduced bowel sounds
steps.x: **NSAID**, abdominal pain, then **confusion**, **hypotension** and a distended tender abdomen. Raised lactate: sepsis from peritonitis.

elim: Causes suprapubic pain and a palpable bladder; not raised lactate with peritonism.
Does not cause this degree of sepsis.
Does not explain the abdominal signs.
A common cause of confusion, but the abdomen is the source here.

steps.x: **D. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Elderly + NSAID + confusion + shock + tender abdomen = think perforated ulcer.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man takes diclofenac for back pain. He vomited a small amount of dark brown, granular material this morning. An hour later he developed sudden severe epigastric pain that has spread across his abdomen. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has board-like rigidity.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: NSAID use, ground-coffee vomiting (bleeding ulcer) and sudden epigastric pain becoming generalised with rigidity is a perforated peptic ulcer.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**NSAID** + **coffee-ground** vomit (an ulcer) + sudden **generalised peritonitis**.

elim: Does not cause coffee-ground vomiting with a board-like abdomen in an NSAID user.
Follows forceful vomiting with chest pain and surgical emphysema.
Fresh blood after retching; no peritonitis.
Large fresh haematemesis in liver disease, without peritonism.

steps.x: **E. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Coffee-ground vomiting then a rigid abdomen in an NSAID user = perforated peptic ulcer.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has had sudden epigastric pain for 6 hours, now generalised, after weeks of taking ibuprofen for a frozen shoulder. She has vomited twice and lies very still. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her abdomen is mildly distended.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of her abdomen?
questions.e: Peritonitis from a perforated ulcer causes a paralysed, distended bowel with reduced or absent bowel sounds.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of her abdomen? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Generalised **peritonitis** paralyses the bowel: quiet abdomen.

elim: Suggests aortic disease, not perforation.
Seen in mechanical obstruction.
Seen in gastroenteritis or early obstruction.
Seen in gastric outlet obstruction.

steps.x: **D. Reduced or absent bowel sounds.** Perforation with peritonitis = reduced or absent bowel sounds.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has a perforated gastric ulcer confirmed at surgery. Her H. pylori test is negative. Her medications are amlodipine, levothyroxine, paracetamol, omeprazole that she stopped 2 months ago, and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily started 3 months ago.
questions.q: Which of her medications is the most likely cause of her ulcer?
questions.e: NSAIDs are the main drug cause of peptic ulcer perforation; with a negative H. pylori test, regular ibuprofen is the culprit.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which of her medications is the most likely cause of her ulcer? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Two main causes: **H. pylori** (negative) and **NSAIDs**.

elim: Not a cause of peptic ulcers.
Not ulcerogenic.
Protective; stopping it removed protection but it does not cause ulcers.
Not ulcerogenic at normal doses.

steps.x: **B. Ibuprofen.** Perforated ulcer + negative H. pylori = NSAID until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had a laparotomy and washout for a perforated sigmoid colon 8 days ago. He was improving but now has swinging fevers up to 39.0°C, rigors and lower abdominal pain. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. CT shows a 6 cm rim-enhancing pelvic fluid collection containing gas.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Abscess formation is a recognised complication of perforation and peritonitis: swinging fever about a week after surgery with a rim-enhancing collection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Swinging fever** a week after surgery for contamination + **rim-enhancing collection**.

elim: He had a washout; the finding is a walled-off collection.
Diarrhoea with colitis, not a rim-enhancing collection.
Distension and vomiting, without swinging fever and a collection.
Superficial; does not cause a deep pelvic collection.

steps.x: **C. Intra-abdominal abscess.** Swinging fever after peritonitis = abscess: image it and drain it.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden severe abdominal pain. He is pale and sweaty. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His abdomen is rigid. He has no cannula and no tests have been done yet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step?
o: ABCDE assessment with urgent surgical review and bloods
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
questions.e: A shocked patient with peritonitis needs an ABCDE assessment, IV access with bloods (including lactate) and urgent surgical review before imaging.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate first step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no tests have been done yet
steps.x: Unstable patient: **assess and resuscitate first**, call the surgeons, then image.

elim: Important, but not before resuscitation and assessment.
The first imaging test, but he needs ABCDE assessment first.
Contraindicated in suspected perforation.
Not the first step.

steps.x: **A. ABCDE assessment with urgent surgical review and bloods.** Suspected perforation in a sick patient: ABCDE + bloods + urgent surgical review first.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has 2 days of increasing lower abdominal pain with fever. She is tender with guarding in the left iliac fossa and lower abdomen. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her erect chest X-ray shows no free air. The surgeons want to know whether, and where, the bowel has perforated.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
Repeat erect chest X-ray in 24 hours
questions.e: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard: most specific, shows extraluminal gas or fluid and locates the site. A normal erect CXR does not exclude perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Normal CXR does **not** exclude it; the surgeons need the **site**.

elim: Contraindicated in suspected perforation.
Contraindicated; insufflation could worsen a perforation.
Delays diagnosis.
Poor for free gas and for the colon.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.** Gold standard for perforation = CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer and is being resuscitated. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. The registrar sends a full blood count, CRP, renal function and amylase, and wants one more test to judge tissue hypoperfusion and how sick he is.
questions.q: Which additional blood test is most appropriate?
questions.e: Raised inflammatory markers and a raised lactate are typical of perforation; lactate reflects hypoperfusion and sepsis severity.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which additional blood test is most appropriate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Severity and **hypoperfusion** = **lactate** (on a blood gas).

elim: Non-specific; not a severity marker here.
Irrelevant to acute severity.
Diagnoses pancreatitis; not a severity marker for perforation.
Not a marker of abdominal sepsis.

steps.x: **C. Lactate.** Perforation bloods: WCC, CRP and lactate.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with sudden severe epigastric pain and peritonism has a CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast. She takes naproxen. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her CT?
o: Target sign in the right abdomen
questions.e: Gas and fluid escape the breached bowel lumen into the peritoneal cavity, so CT shows extraluminal gas and fluid: a surgical emergency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on her CT? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
NSAID + sudden epigastric peritonitis = perforation. On CT, contents and gas are **outside** the bowel.

elim: A sign of bowel ischaemia or colitis.
Cholecystitis.
Severe pancreatitis.
Intussusception.

steps.x: **B. Extraluminal gas and free fluid.** CT in perforation = extraluminal gas and free fluid.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman takes ibuprofen and aspirin. She has 4 hours of sudden severe epigastric pain. She is tender with guarding in the epigastrium. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. She has been assessed, cannulated and bloods have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.e: An erect chest X-ray is the initial investigation in suspected perforated peptic ulcer, looking for pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**NSAIDs** + sudden epigastric peritonism: suspected perforated ulcer. First image looks for **free air**.

elim: Poor at detecting free gas.
Not an emergency first-line test.
Contraindicated in suspected perforation.
Free air is far harder to see than on an erect film.

steps.x: **B. Erect chest X-ray.** Suspected perforated ulcer: erect CXR first, CT if it is normal but suspicion remains.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer on CT and is awaiting theatre. He has been given oxygen, analgesia and IV antibiotics. He feels nauseated and has vomited bile three times in the last hour. His abdomen is distended.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional measure?
o: Encourage small sips of clear fluid
questions.e: First-line care for perforation is NBM, IV fluids, oxygen, IV antibiotics and analgesia, with an NG tube if there is nausea or vomiting to decompress the stomach.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional measure? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Vomiting and distension in a patient who is **NBM**: decompress the stomach.

elim: He must be nil by mouth.
Avoid prokinetics in suspected perforation or obstruction.
He is vomiting and nil by mouth.
Not indicated.

steps.x: **C. Nasogastric tube insertion.** Perforation with nausea or vomiting = NG tube.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a perforated sigmoid colon on CT. She is nil by mouth with IV fluids and oxygen, and has had IV morphine. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. She is booked for theatre.
questions.q: Which drug is most important to give now?
questions.e: Faecal contamination of the peritoneum needs broad-spectrum IV antibiotics as part of first-line management, alongside NBM, fluids, oxygen and analgesia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which drug is most important to give now? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Faecal** contamination and fever: bacterial peritonitis needs **broad-spectrum IV** cover.

elim: No indication such as adrenal insufficiency.
A prokinetic; avoid.
Too narrow and oral; she is nil by mouth.
NSAIDs are a cause of perforation, and she is nil by mouth.

steps.x: **A. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.** Perforation first-line: NBM, IV fluids, oxygen, analgesia and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has a small bowel perforation from a seatbelt injury, confirmed on CT. He has been resuscitated and given IV antibiotics. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His abdomen is generalised tender with guarding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Conservative management with IV antibiotics alone
Urgent laparotomy with repair or resection and washout
questions.e: GI perforation needs urgent surgery: repair, resection or washout as appropriate. A small bowel tear is repaired or the segment resected.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Free **small bowel** perforation with peritonitis: source control in theatre.

elim: Free perforation with peritonitis needs surgery.
There is no discrete collection.
An operation for the sigmoid colon.
Used for perforated peptic ulcers.

steps.x: **E. Urgent laparotomy with repair or resection and washout.** Perforation definitive treatment = urgent surgery (repair, resection, washout).

questions.stem: An 80 year old man is having an emergency laparotomy for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with faecal contamination. He is on noradrenaline. The consultant decides to perform a Hartmann's procedure and the student is asked to describe it.
questions.q: Which best describes this operation?
o: Resection with end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump
Resection with primary anastomosis and no stoma
questions.e: Hartmann's procedure resects the diseased sigmoid, brings out an end colostomy and closes the rectal stump, avoiding an anastomosis in a contaminated, septic field.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best describes this operation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Contaminated** field + **septic shock**: remove the segment and **avoid an anastomosis**.

elim: This is the repair for a perforated peptic ulcer.
Avoided in a contaminated, unstable patient.
For right-sided colonic disease.
Leaves the perforated segment in place.

steps.x: **B. Resection with end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump.** Hartmann's = sigmoid resection + end colostomy + rectal stump closure.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has sudden severe abdominal pain. She takes naproxen. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Her abdomen is rigid. She has had 1 litre of IV fluid and IV antibiotics with little change. Her erect chest X-ray is shown.

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Crescents of gas under both hemidiaphragms: pneumoperitoneum.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Admit to the ward for observation
CT abdomen and pelvis before any decision
questions.e: Hypotension, sepsis and peritonitis with free air is a surgical emergency needing immediate intervention; do not delay for further imaging.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Hypotension + sepsis + peritonitis** with **free air** on the CXR: no time for more scans.

elim: She is in septic shock with peritonitis.
With free air, shock and peritonitis, theatre should not be delayed.
Contraindicated in perforation.
Inadequate and she is nil by mouth.

steps.x: **C. Emergency laparotomy.** Shocked + peritonitis + free air = immediate surgery.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman has large bowel obstruction from a sigmoid tumour. She has colicky pain, absolute constipation and marked distension, and she is vomiting. She is nil by mouth with IV fluids and an NG tube. The nurse asks for an antiemetic.
questions.q: Which antiemetic should be avoided?
questions.e: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic dopamine antagonist; in mechanical obstruction it increases pressure behind the blockage and can precipitate perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which antiemetic should be avoided? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Mechanical obstruction**: avoid anything that drives the bowel harder against the blockage.

elim: An antihistamine; generally acceptable in obstruction.
Acts centrally; acceptable in obstruction.
Broad-spectrum; used in obstruction.
A 5-HT3 antagonist; acceptable.

steps.x: **D. Metoclopramide.** Mechanical bowel obstruction: avoid metoclopramide (perforation risk).

questions.stem: A 46 year old man had a laparoscopic omental patch repair of a perforated duodenal ulcer 2 days ago. He does not take NSAIDs. A biopsy taken at surgery is positive for Helicobacter pylori. He is now eating and recovering well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate further management?
questions.e: After omental patch repair, the cause must be treated: H. pylori eradication (PPI plus two antibiotics) to prevent recurrence. NSAIDs should be avoided.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate further management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The perforation is fixed; now treat **the cause**: **H. pylori**.

elim: Steroids increase ulcer risk.
Not needed; the ulcer is repaired and the cause treatable.
NSAIDs cause ulcers.
Not a recognised step.

steps.x: **A. H. pylori eradication therapy.** After repair of a perforated ulcer: treat the cause (eradicate H. pylori, stop NSAIDs).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer. His erect chest X-ray shows a crescent of gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm. He has been sitting upright in the department for 15 minutes. A medical student asks why the gas collects there.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this finding?
o: Gas from bacterial fermentation in the liver
Gas has escaped the bowel lumen and risen in the peritoneal cavity
Lung air leaking across the diaphragm
Normal gas in the gastric fundus
Swallowed air trapped in the duodenum
questions.e: Gas escapes the perforated lumen into the peritoneal cavity and rises to lie under the diaphragm in an upright patient: the classic sign of perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for this finding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: crescent of gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm
steps.x: The gas is **outside** the bowel, in the **peritoneal cavity**, and rises in an erect patient.

elim: Not a cause of a subdiaphragmatic crescent.
That would be a pneumothorax.
The fundus lies under the left hemidiaphragm, within the stomach wall.
Air inside bowel is not free air.

steps.x: **B. Gas has escaped the bowel lumen and risen in the peritoneal cavity.** Free air under the diaphragm = gas escaped from a perforated lumen.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a perforated duodenal ulcer. Within minutes of the perforation she had severe pain and a rigid abdomen. At surgery 3 hours later, the peritoneal fluid is bile-stained and cultures grow no organisms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her early peritonitis?
o: Chemical peritonitis from gastric acid and bile
questions.e: A full-thickness breach lets luminal contents into the peritoneum: from the stomach and duodenum, acid and bile cause chemical peritonitis first, then bacterial peritonitis develops later.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her early peritonitis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Immediate, **sterile**, bile-stained: acid and bile irritate the peritoneum **chemically**.

elim: The duodenum has few bacteria and cultures are sterile.
The fluid is bile-stained, not blood.
Not the mechanism of ulcer perforation.
Occurs in ascites, without a perforation.

steps.x: **B. Chemical peritonitis from gastric acid and bile.** Upper GI perforation = early chemical peritonitis; colonic perforation = bacterial/faecal peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer. He does not take NSAIDs. A urea breath test is positive. A student asks how this infection led to a full-thickness hole in the duodenum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct bacterial invasion through all layers of the wall
Impaired mucosal barrier allowing acid-peptic digestion of the wall
Toxin-mediated bowel wall necrosis of Peyer's patches
questions.e: H. pylori (and NSAIDs) impair the mucosal protective barrier, allowing acid and pepsin to digest through the full thickness of the wall.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**H. pylori** damages the **protective barrier**; **acid and pepsin** do the digging.

elim: H. pylori does not invade full thickness.
That is intestinal ischaemia.
Acid is needed for peptic ulceration.
That is typhoid.

steps.x: **B. Impaired mucosal barrier allowing acid-peptic digestion of the wall.** Peptic perforation = loss of mucosal protection + acid-peptic digestion through the wall.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has had faecal peritonitis from a perforated sigmoid colon for 18 hours. His peripheries are warm and flushed. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 134 bpm, BP 76/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His lactate is 6.2 mmol/L. His BP has not improved after 2 litres of IV fluid.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypotension?
o: Septic shock from a systemic inflammatory response
questions.e: Bacterial peritonitis triggers a systemic inflammatory response with vasodilation and capillary leak: septic shock, which can develop rapidly and is a reason to avoid anastomosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypotension? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Contamination + **warm** peripheries + **fluid-refractory** hypotension + high lactate: **distributive** shock.

elim: Peripheries would be cold, with no clear source.
No bleeding; peripheries would be cold.
Would respond to 2 litres of fluid and peripheries would be cold.
Follows spinal cord injury.

steps.x: **E. Septic shock from a systemic inflammatory response.** Fluid-refractory hypotension with warm peripheries after perforation = septic shock.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has small bowel obstruction from adhesions. He is vomiting and a junior doctor prescribes IV metoclopramide. He has colicky pain, distension and has not passed flatus for 2 days. The pharmacist advises against it and suggests cyclizine instead.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for the pharmacist's advice?
o: It causes QT prolongation in all patients
It increases peristalsis against the obstruction, raising pressure
It is ineffective in vomiting of any cause

questions.e: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and prokinetic. In mechanical obstruction it drives peristalsis against the blockage, raising intraluminal pressure and risking perforation.
